new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work was listed and the compiler marked it silent; I opened it and re-read it in full (text plus rendered pages 4, 6, 7) rather than spot-checking. Nothing on stress was missed. No new works added; the other files already held in the folder (Blench 2019 Atlas, Mainz Tula-Waja page, 100-wordlist scanned, Pronouns-and-Numbers sheet, Adelberger & Blench 2026) were consulted only to settle Tso's subgroup and were confirmed by earlier passes to contain no stress statement.

sources.citation: Kleinewillinghöfer, Ulrich. 2020. Waja. In Rainer Vossen & Gerrit J. Dimmendaal (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of African Languages, 507-520. Oxford: OUP. doi:10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199609895.013.35.
sources.note: FOR WAJA, NOT TSO: §39.2.3 Tone (p. 509) states two tonemes H and L, a non-high surface level from pausal lowering, TBU = vowels and syllabic consonants, falling = H+L on one TBU, tone mainly grammatical (aspect/mood, valence, class pronouns and suffixes), floating tones and downstep; fn. 4 gives phrase-initial/final H lowering to NH. No stress/accent statement on the page (the waja1259 record reports none in pp. 508-510 either).
sources.venue: The Oxford Handbook of African Languages

The words stress/accent/tone/tonal/pitch/syllable do not occur in the linguistic sense anywhere in the 34 pages (checked on the full text). sources.citation: Kleinewillinghöfer, Ulrich. 2010. Jalaa, the last member of an extinct language family. Draft manuscript, 12 pp; paper presented at the Workshop 'Language Isolates in Africa', Laboratoire Dynamique du Langage, Institut des Sciences de l'Homme, Lyon, 3-4 December 2010. Glottolog reference 44125 (provider hh; languages coded Jalaa [cet] and Komta, not Tso). Cited as 'Kleinewillinghöfer n.d. [manuscript]' in Adelberger & Blench 2026 (AAeO). English Wikipedia (Jalaa language) describes it as a revised version of the 2001 SUGIA 16/17 article, which is in our rows; Glottolog and Adelberger & Blench list the two separately.

sources.access_detail: in print; no library copy located
sources.note: The only located document said to discuss Tso dialect phonology first-hand (pp. 4-6: phonological peculiarities distinguishing the Tso dialects, attributed to substrate contact); whether these peculiarities are segmental or tonal is not established. Kleinewillinghöfer transcribes Tso with H/L (and falling) tone marks in all his published Tso data, so any phonological discussion by him presupposes a tonal analysis, but no tone inventory statement is confirmed.
